General Stilwell, chief of staff to Chiang Kai-shek, issued paper C.C.S. 405 at Cairo on 22 November 1943 under the title Role of China in Defeat of Japan. It answers a direct question: what operations mounted from China would most affect the course of the Pacific war.

His ladder of operations starts with helping in north Burma and building the land route to China. It runs through very-long-range bombing of Japan in early 1944. Then come the recapture of Canton and Hong Kong in the winter of 1944 and 1945. An attack on Formosa follows if needed by May 1945. Stilwell claims the plan is cheap, clashes with no other theater, and could cut a year or two off the Quebec timetable for Japan's defeat. It asks for three American divisions earmarked for China.

Military chiefs rarely wrote as a body to the diplomats. Such a letter signals questions where war plans met foreign policy. In September 1944, those questions centered on Germany's defeat. They also touched the campaign against Japan. For readers, the message shows the armed services stating a joint view. The State Department received it while summit briefings were being finished.
frus-1944-quebec-d182:
Harry Dexter White recorded the meeting of September 14, 1944, between Morgenthau and Lord Cherwell, the session Roosevelt had arranged. Cherwell took lend-lease first, outlining British needs for the period between Germany's defeat and Japan's. A cut of 27 percent in American aid, he suggested, would appear reasonable to the British.

Morgenthau rejected fixing aid by percentages; the question, he said, was how much munitions Britain needed for her Pacific role. Both men liked a joint committee, and White and MacDougall were set to drafting its directive. On Germany, Cherwell doubted American labor would approve so drastic a program. Morgenthau framed the choice bluntly: a strong Germany and weak England, or the reverse. He chose the reverse.
frus-1944-quebec-d282: A secretaries' note dated September 19, 1944, records the final approval of the Japan planning date. Roosevelt and Churchill approved the Combined Chiefs' recommendation. arxiv-2606-07182: Generating audio for video — with a reference sound's timbre and tempo — is the goal. Audio Imitator controls both in video-to-audio synthesis with an audio reference. The imitation matches the reference's sonic character. Reference sounds guide generation. Timbre transfer works for video.
arxiv-2606-07282: IoT intrusion detection usually watches routing metrics — but radio features add signal. This paper rethinks detection by augmenting routing with radio features. The augmentation catches attacks the network layer misses. Network-layer blind spots get covered by radio. Physical-layer signals reveal hidden intruders.
arxiv-2606-07382: Covariance matrices estimated from little data need shrinkage — and stochastic interpolation provides it. This paper shrinks covariance via that interpolation. The shrinkage stabilizes high-dimensional estimates. High-dimensional covariance estimation needs strong regularization. Stochastic interpolation provides welcome stability. Stability is essential.
arxiv-2606-07582: Predicting customer churn on structured data — with FT-Transformer and stacking ensembles. This paper does it. The ensembles squeeze signal from tables.  Business customer retention fundamentally depends on churn prediction. Transformer ensembles extract meaningful predictive signal from structured tabular data.
tob-4282:
Apollodorus of Athens gets credit for the Library, the ancient world's own handbook of Greek mythology. Gods, heroes, and their tangled families march in order from the first beings to the Trojan War and the heroes' returns. James George Frazer translated it for the Loeb series in 1921, with rich notes.

A student who needs to know how Heracles ties to Perseus, or which king fathered which monster-slayer, finds the answer here in plain prose. The Library lacks poetry; it offers system instead, which scholars crave. Verified from the 1919 edition record, Frazer's Apollodorus remains antiquity's one-stop reference for its own myths.
st-osyth-true-just-recorde-1582:
A True and Just Recorde gives the full account of the witch trials at St Osyth in Essex in 1582. Fourteen people faced charges there, in the largest witch case of Queen Elizabeth's reign. The pamphlet prints the charges, the witness statements, and the confessions at length.

Because the record is so full, readers can follow how each charge was built. Neighbors tell of lost beasts, sick children, and sudden deaths blamed on hidden malice. The court sorts the claims and sends some of the accused to the gallows. No Elizabethan witch case left a richer paper trail.
joan-buts-tryal-examination-1682:
Late in England's witchcraft era, a court set Joan Buts free. An Account of the Tryal and Examination of Joan Buts, printed as a broadside in 1682, tells how. Most trial prints end at the gallows, so an acquittal on the page is rare.

The sheet records the charge against her, the proof brought in, and the way the court weighed it. By 1682 judges and juries were growing harder to sway with tales of spells and spirits. More of the accused were walking free, and this case shows why. The broadside marks the slow turn of the tide against the panic.
jane-kent-old-bailey-1682:
London's Old Bailey heard the case of Jane Kent in June 1682, and a sessions paper tells it in full. A Full and True Account of the Proceedings at the Old Bailey prints the court's work for that term. Kent's witchcraft charge sat among the usual run of thefts and killings.

The report gives her charge, the proof laid against her, and the court's verdict in plain order. That a London court still tried witches so late surprises many readers. Yet the record shows the charge alive in the capital decades past the panic's height. The paper is a plain, rare look at a city trial.
bideford-witches-tryal-1682:
Three women of Bideford in Devon were hanged in 1682, the last people put to death for witchcraft in England. The Tryal, Condemnation, and Execution of Three Witches at Bideford records their end. Temperance Lloyd stands first among the names the pamphlet preserves.

The print lays out the claims against them: sickness, fits, and shapes seen by night. It follows the case from charge to gallows in the plain style of the day. No English court would hang a witch again after this Devon case. The pamphlet thus closes a two-hundred-year run of trials in print.
bideford-witches-relation-1682:
Bideford's 1682 trial produced a second, fuller print beside the short trial pamphlet. A True and Impartial Relation of the Informations against Three Witches sets out the sworn claims in more depth. Together the two prints give the whole case, charge by charge.

Witness after witness tells of pains, threats, and strange sights laid to the accused women. The detail lets readers weigh what the Devon court had to weigh. It also shows how much print a single late case could still draw. Read as a pair, the Bideford prints end England's witch story in full.
bideford-witches-ballad-1682:
Street singers carried the Bideford case to crowds who never saw a trial print. Witchcraft Discovered and Punished, a ballad of 1682, turns the last English witch executions into song. Broadside ballads were the cheap news and music of the street in those years.

In short rhymed verses, the ballad tells the charges, the trial, and the deaths of the three women. Its tune and tale were made to stick in the mind and pass mouth to mouth. The song shows how the news of a trial lived on outside the court. It is the folk echo of a famous case.
kojiki-chamberlain-1882:
Japan's oldest chronicle, the Kojiki, was set down in the year 712. Basil Hall Chamberlain made the first English version in 1882. The work tells how the gods made the islands and ruled the sky and sea. It then traces the line of early emperors.

Myths crowd the first part, with the storm god, the sun goddess, and tricks and fights among the gods. Songs sit inside the prose, some of them very old. Later parts turn to court tales, births, deaths, and wars. The Kojiki stands at the root of Shinto myth and of Japanese letters as a whole.
newbrough-oahspe-new-bible-1882:
John Ballou Newbrough said spirits drove his hands on a new type craft. Oahspe came out in 1882 as a new Bible for a new age. Newbrough was a New York dentist and a man of the spirit creed. The book calls its age the Kosmon era, a time of light.

Vast tales tell of gods, heavens, and the rise and fall of lands now sunk. A Book of Cosmogony lays out the make of the sky and of man. Old lands such as Atlantis take a large share of the tale. The book is the great said text of the spirit line in the States.
sbe-17-vinaya-texts-2-1882:
Book Seventeen of the Sacred Books of the East came out in 1882. It holds Part Two of the Vinaya Texts in the dress of Rhys Davids and Oldenberg. The Vinaya is the rule book of the monks of the Buddha. Part One gave the core rules and the first books of the Mahavagga.

Here the Mahavagga runs from Book Five to Book Ten. The Kullavagga then starts, with Books One to Three in this part. Rules deal with dress, food, the rains rest, and strife in the host. The book is a dry text with rich worth for the tale of the faith.
strindberg-lucky-pehr-1882:
August Strindberg wrote Lucky Pehr in 1882, an allegorical five-act fairy play, here in Velma Swanston Howard's translation. Howard's authorized translation carried Strindberg's most performed early play to English-speaking stages and readers in print. The play mixes folk tale, satire, and dream in a form all Strindberg's own at twenty-three.

Pehr, a church verger's son, finds a ring that grants wishes and rides luck up the world. He tries wealth, fame, and love, and each gift sours in his hands by the tale's logic. A cathedral tower, a talking statue, and a chorus of townsfolk frame his rise and fall in life. At last he renounces the ring and chooses honest work and love without magic's false ease and shine. The fable's charm hides a sharp moral on ambition that Strindberg never outgrew in art.
bunyan-holy-war-1682:
Bunyan's Holy War, published in 1682, tells the story of Mansoul, a town built for its lord Shaddai and seized by the giant Diabolus. It is an allegory, a tale in which the town stands for the human soul. Only Pilgrim's Progress outsold it among Bunyan's works in his lifetime.

Emmanuel, the prince, besieges the town, wins it back, and then must hold it against fresh plots from within and without. Every gate, captain, and council maps onto a faculty or trial of the inner life. Puritan families read it as the great companion piece to the Pilgrim's story.
blagrave-introduction-to-astrology-1682:
Joseph Blagrave was an astrologer and physician in Reading whose Introduction to Astrology appeared in 1682. He practiced physic by the stars, choosing treatments from the patient's chart as much as from the symptoms. His book is a plain guide to the art for beginners.

Blagrave teaches the signs, planets, and houses, then shows how to judge sickness, theft, marriage, and travel by horary charts. His cases come from his own practice among Berkshire farmers and tradesmen. The introduction shows astrology as a working country trade, not a courtly mystery. His plain speech assumes no Latin and little money for books.
donnelly-atlantis-the-antediluvian-world:
Ignatius Donnelly, an American writer and former congressman, published Atlantis: The Antediluvian World in 1882. Donnelly argued that Atlantis, the lost island in Plato's dialogues, was a real place and a real early state. He claimed its people spread farming, myth, and building across the world before a flood destroyed them.

Donnelly compared myths, alphabets, plants, and ruins from Egypt, Europe, and the Americas to build his case. He treated similar flood stories and sun worship as traces of one lost source. Scholars rejected most of his proof, but the book launched the modern Atlantis craze and still defines how lost-continent claims are argued.
stanton-history-woman-suffrage-vol-2-188:
Volume 2 of History of Woman Suffrage appeared in 1882, edited by Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Susan B Anthony, and Matilda Joslyn Gage. The volume covers 1861 to 1876, years when the movement split and reorganized. The editors again built the history from speeches, letters, and reports.

War work by women, the fight over the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments, and the founding of rival suffrage groups fill the record. The editors' own National Woman Suffrage Association stands at the center of their telling. State campaigns and early votes, including women voting in western territories, get full documentation. The volume preserves the words of a movement arguing with itself and with the nation.
stevenson-new-arabian-nights-1882:
Robert Louis Stevenson modeled The New Arabian Nights on the old tales of Harun al-Rashid wandering Baghdad in disguise. He published the stories in magazines, then as his first book, in 1882. The setting is not Baghdad but gaslit Victorian London.

Prince Florizel of Bohemia roams London at night hunting adventure, with his loyal colonel at his side. In The Suicide Club he infiltrates a society where tired men draw cards for death. A second cycle follows a diamond stolen and passed from hand to hand. Stevenson mixes danger with wry humor and polished style. The book launched his career as a teller of tales.
gautier-cleopatras-nights-hearn-1882:
Théophile Gautier wrote tales of ghosts, vampires, and living mummies for French readers in the mid-1800s. Lafcadio Hearn translated six of them into lush English in 1882. The lead tale, One of Cleopatra's Nights, imagines a poor Egyptian youth granted one night with the queen, at the price of his life.

Other tales give Clarimonde, a courtesan who returns from the dead, and Arria Marcella, a spirit met among the ruins of Pompeii. The Mummy's Foot turns a comic purchase into a dream of ancient Egypt. Gautier mixes beauty with dread in rich, exact prose. These stories helped found the French literature of the fantastic.
fontane-irrungen-wirrungen-1882:
Theodor Fontane's Berlin novel Irrungen, Wirrungen appeared in German in 1888 from an 1882 serial start, and Katharine Royce Englished it in 1917. Her version, Trials and Tribulations, ran in the Harvard Classics Shelf of Fiction. Lene, a seamstress, loves Botho, a young baron and officer, across the class line of Berlin.

Both know the match cannot last, and both accept its end with quiet grace. Fontane tells the parting without villains, blame, or melodrama. Talk, walks, and small social signs carry the whole weight of feeling. The novel is often called the finest German story of love across class. Its restraint is the source of its lasting power.
i-ching-legge-1882:
James Legge translated the Yi King, the I Ching or Classic of Changes, into English in 1882. His complete version appeared as volume sixteen of the Sacred Books of the East. The Chinese classic builds its counsel from sixty-four hexagrams, figures of six broken and unbroken lines used in divination.

Legge gives each hexagram with its ancient judgments, the Tuan and Hsiang comments, and the appendices called the Ten Wings. King Wen and the Duke of Chou stand behind the oldest layers, by tradition. The book served China as oracle, philosophy, and mirror of change for two thousand years. Legge's laborious version long anchored English study of it. His notes map the text with Victorian thoroughness.
yusuf-zulaikha-jami-griffith-1882:
Ralph T. H. Griffith translated Jami's Yusuf and Zulaikha into English verse in 1882, for Trubner's Oriental Series. Jami, the last great classical poet of Persia, retold the story of Joseph and Potiphar's wife in the 1400s. The Quran and Persian tradition had already made Zulaikha's love a figure of the soul's longing for God.

Griffith follows Jami through Joseph's beauty, his trials, and Zulaikha's long, refining passion. In Sufi reading, her desire is purified until it becomes devotion itself. The Victorian rendering became the classic English dress of the poem. Griffith, known for his Ramayana and Rigveda versions, brought the same care here. The romance remains the crown of Jami's seven poems.
rubaiyat-khayyam-whinfield-1882:
E. H. Whinfield published his Quatrains of Omar Khayyam in 1882, in Trubner's Oriental Series, with the Persian text and English verse on facing terms. Where Fitzgerald had chosen and reshaped a hundred quatrains into a famous poem, Whinfield gives all five hundred. His version is the full scholarly alternative, with introduction and notes.

Wine, roses, brief life, and the turning heavens fill quatrain after quatrain. Some praise pleasure; others mock the learned and the pious alike. Readers can watch Khayyam's thought range wider than Fitzgerald's selection suggests. Whinfield, an Indian civil servant and Persian scholar, translated closely rather than freely. Students still set his completeness beside Fitzgerald's art.
muallaqat-jones-1782:
William Jones published The Moallakat in 1782, the first English rendering of the Mu'allaqat, the seven suspended odes of pre-Islamic Arabia. The odes, by poets such as Imru al-Qais, Tarafa, and Zuhayr, were said to have hung in the Kaaba at Mecca for their excellence. Jones adds a preliminary discourse on Arabian poetry and full philological notes.

Each ode moves from a halted campsite's ruins to love, boast, desert travel, and tribal war. Camels, storms, and night journeys carry some of the finest early Arabic verse. Jones learned Arabic and Persian in India and reshaped British knowledge of Eastern tongues. This translation began his fame as an Orientalist. The odes still open every history of Arabic poetry.
machiavelli-writings-detmold-vol-1-1882:
Christian E Detmold's translation of Niccolò Machiavelli's writings, issued from 1882 to 1891 in four volumes, opens here with volume one. Machiavelli, the Florentine secretary of the early 1500s, changed how the world thinks about power. Detmold gathered his historical, political, and diplomatic writings into one English set, and this volume begins it.

Across the full set stand the Discourses, the Florentine Histories, The Art of War, comedies, letters, and state papers. Machiavelli writes about republics, princes, armies, and fortune with cold clarity. His name became a byword, yet the full range of his work is wider and wiser than the legend. Volume one starts the complete English Machiavelli of the Victorian age.
machiavelli-writings-detmold-vol-2-1882:
Volume two continues Detmold's English Machiavelli, the four-volume set of 1882 to 1891. Niccolò Machiavelli wrote in the thick of Italy's wars and invasions, serving Florence as envoy and militia planner. His Historical, Political, and Diplomatic Writings, as Detmold titled the set, hold nearly everything he left.

The works gathered across these volumes run from the Discourses on Rome to the Florentine Histories and The Art of War. Letters and diplomatic reports show the thinker at work, reading courts and captains. Machiavelli founded modern political thought by describing power as it is, not as preachers wished it. This second volume keeps that full portrait building, in Detmold's sturdy English.
machiavelli-writings-detmold-vol-3-1882:
Detmold's Machiavelli reaches volume three of four, in the English set issued from 1882 to 1891. Niccolò Machiavelli, Florence's sharp-eyed secretary, had been dead three centuries, yet his writings still started arguments in every capital. The set presents his historical, political, and diplomatic works whole, rather than the single famous book, The Prince, alone.

Plays and letters stand in the set beside the Discourses, the histories, and the writings on war. That mix matters: Machiavelli the comic playwright and the fond letter writer round out Machiavelli the analyst of power. Volume three carries the reader deeper into that complete figure. Few political writers reward a full reading more, or punish a partial one less fairly.
machiavelli-writings-detmold-vol-4-1882:
Volume four completes Christian E Detmold's translation of Machiavelli's Historical, Political, and Diplomatic Writings. The set ran from 1882 to 1891. With this volume, English readers gained the whole Machiavelli in four books: Discourses, Florentine Histories, and The Art of War. Comedies, letters, and papers of state stand beside them.

Niccolò Machiavelli watched republics rise and princes fall, and wrote down the rules he saw beneath the chaos. His clear, hard teaching on power made him the founder of modern political thought. The closing volume finishes the fullest English Machiavelli of its century. Readers who end here hold the complete case, from statecraft to stage comedy, in one author's hand.
hobbes-behemoth-1682:
Behemoth: or, The Long Parliament is Thomas Hobbes's history of the English Civil War, written in dialogue and published in 1682. Four parts carry an old man's account of how England fell into rebellion between 1640 and 1660. Hobbes, who had fled to Paris when the war began, watched his country's ruin from exile and thought hard about its causes.

The dialogue blames seditious preaching, ambitious parliament men, and universities that taught men to love dispute. Against the chaos stands Hobbes's remedy: one sovereign power, feared and obeyed. Behemoth is Leviathan turned historian, applying its doctrine to fresh wounds. Hobbes's king had kept the work back; its 1682 printing let England judge the old man's verdict.
stephen-science-ethics-1882:
Leslie Stephen wrote The Science of Ethics in 1882, bringing Darwin's theory to bear on moral life. Stephen was a leading man of letters and a frank agnostic. He asked whether ethics could rest on science rather than on church command. The book was his most sustained work of philosophy.

Stephen traces moral rules to the health and survival of the social group. Feelings of right and wrong, he argues, grow as societies grow. He tests his view against rival schools, including the utilitarians he partly followed. The result is a calm, tough piece of Victorian thought. It helped set terms for later ethics.
hering-guiding-symptoms-vol6-1882:
In 1882 the sixth volume of Hering's Guiding Symptoms joined the growing row on prescribers' shelves. The work stands as the great American materia medica of its school. Its plan does not change here: remedies in order, symptoms grouped by the part of the body they touch.

Editors working from Hering's own papers shaped the entries with care. They kept his signs for confirmed and characteristic symptoms, the marks a busy reader scans for first. A lifetime of provings stands behind the terse lines, each one earned in tests on healthy volunteers. Doctors treated the whole set as a final court when brief handbooks gave too little.
sarva-darsana-samgraha-cowell-gough-1882:
E. B. Cowell and A. E. Gough translated Madhava's Sarva-Darsana-Samgraha in 1882, a learned review of India's systems of thought. Madhavacharya, a fourteenth-century scholar and minister, surveys sixteen schools in rising order of truth as he sees it. Materialists, Buddhists, Jains, and the great Hindu systems each get a fair, careful statement of their claims and proofs.

The survey climbs toward the author's own Advaita Vedanta, which the last chapter crowns above the rest. Few books let a reader compare Indian philosophies in their own terms so compactly and so clearly. The translation remains a standard guide to the darsanas, the viewpoints that shaped India's intellectual history for centuries.
genji-suematsu-1882:
Kencho Suematsu carried The Tale of Genji into English in 1882, the first rendering of Murasaki Shikibu's masterpiece. His version gives chapters one to seventeen, abridged, of the long tale of Prince Genji and the Heian court. Suematsu, a Japanese scholar-diplomat, presented his country's classic to a West that knew nothing of it.

Genji's loves, exiles, and refinements unfold in a world of poetry contests and scented letters. Many call the Genji the world's first novel, and its portrait of court life has no early rival. Suematsu's landmark effort opened that world, however partially, to English readers.
nordenskiold-voyage-vega-vol1-1882:
Adolf Erik Nordenskiöld, a Finnish-Swedish geologist and sailor, took the steamer Vega along Siberia's Arctic coast in 1878. Volume One of The Voyage of the Vega, in its 1882 English form, opens the story. The Northeast Passage had beaten sailors for three centuries.

Nordenskiöld sails from Norway past the great Siberian rivers, mapping coasts and collecting fossils and plants. He meets the Chukchi people of the far northeast with respect and care. Late in the season the Vega freezes in, just short of the Bering Strait. The volume ends with a winter of science and patience among the ice.
plos-pone-0003382:
Vanila F. Palmeira and co-authors tested HIV drugs against a fungus in this 2008 study. The fungus Fonsecaea pedrosoi causes chromoblastomycosis, a long-lasting skin disease. Current drugs for it are harsh, and the fungus often resists them. The team tried drugs that block HIV peptidase enzymes on the fungus instead.

In lab tests, those drugs slowed key steps in the life of the fungus. They also cut traits the fungus needs to cause disease. Using proven HIV drugs this way could speed up treatment options. The paper offers a fresh lead for a neglected tropical disease.
plos-pone-0003482:
Kerstin Schneider, Ursula Meyer-Koenig, and Frank T. Hufert studied a virus that dulls immune alarms in this 2008 paper. Human cytomegalovirus infects most people and hides for life. Plasmacytoid dendritic cells are the body's main source of type I interferon. Most of those cells sit in lymphoid organs.

The team showed the virus impairs those cells inside such organs. A weaker interferon alarm gives the virus room to persist. Muting the sentinels is a classic pathogen survival move. The finding clarifies one way this virus evades its host. This virus infects most adults for life, usually without causing clear illness.
plos-pone-0003582:
Caio Maximino examined a brain structure's evolution in fish and kin in this 2008 paper. The tectum sits in the roof of the vertebrate midbrain. It is often taken as highly conserved across evolution. Maximino assessed three hypotheses about its layered structure in nontetrapods.

He used a cladistic approach, grouping animals by shared traits. Changes in lamination and cell architecture were traced across lineages. Complexity in the tectum did change over time. The result complicates the story of a structure long assumed frozen. Fish vision is a strong test case for how brains change with habitat.
plos-pone-0003682:
Åsa Andersson, Magnus Isaksson, Judit Wefer, and colleagues published this immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. A DNA vaccine encoding a piece of myelin protein can suppress a rat disease that models multiple sclerosis. The authors studied how that vaccine changes the immune attack behind the disease.

They found the vaccine impairs responses of T helper 17 cells, a type that drives the attack on the nervous system. Weaker Th17 responses went with weaker disease in the model. The result shows DNA vaccination can retune a misfiring immune response rather than just block it.
plos-pone-0003782:
Pablo Blinder, Joshua Cove, Maytal Foox, and colleagues published this brain development study in PLOS ONE in 2008. How axons spread their connections along dendrites is a basic open question in neuroscience. The team found signs, in dishes and in living animals, that dendrites help set the density and strength of their own inputs.

They report convergence among dendritic branches that are not sisters of one another. Activity itself controls this coming together, strengthening network connectivity along used paths. The finding shows developing circuits reinforcing the routes they actually use as they wire up.
plos-pone-0003882:
Arjen E. Van't Hof, František Marec, Ilik J. Saccheri, and co-authors mapped the chromosomes of a butterfly in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article concerns Bicyclus anynana, a species widely used in lab studies. For all its use, its chromosomes had drawn little study before this work. The team set out to describe them in full.

They combined direct chromosome study with genetic linkage mapping using AFLP markers. The map covers all 28 chromosomes known from cell counts. A full map helps other labs tie traits to genes in this butterfly. It strengthens a model species used to study wing patterns and evolution.
plos-pone-0003982:
Stuart Jackson, Fred Cummins, and Nuala Brady timed flips in a reversible moving figure in 2008. Some images can be seen two ways, and perception swaps between them. A biological motion figure, like a walking person, is one such case. The authors studied how fast those swaps happen.

Their PLOS ONE article compares biological motion with other moving figures. Timing patterns reveal how the brain settles and unsettles a percept. A walking figure may flip at its own characteristic pace. The work adds to models of how perception stays stable, then changes. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004082:
John Paul Eichorst, Shaoying Lu, Jing Xu, and co-authors measured a cell movement switch in 2008. RhoA is a molecular switch that helps cells crawl and change shape. Biosensors using FRET light transfer can watch RhoA in live cells. Large image sets from those sensors need automated analysis.

Their PLOS ONE article compares RhoA dynamics in moving and still cells. Automated image analysis made the comparison consistent across many cells. Migratory cells showed different RhoA patterns from stationary ones. The method lets labs quantify movement signals without hand scoring. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004182:
Lingyun Zhu and colleagues published this vascular study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Atherosclerosis, the hardening and narrowing of arteries, grows partly through the rapid multiplication of vascular smooth muscle cells in vessel walls. Diabetes raises the risk, since high blood sugar drives these muscle cells to grow and move.

The team focused on PGC-1α, a regulator of cell energy use. They report that it is a key controller of the growth and movement that glucose triggers in these cells. The finding ties a metabolic regulator to the vessel damage that makes diabetes so dangerous for the heart.
plos-pone-0004282:
Hoau-Yan Wang and Lindsay Burns published this pain pharmacology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Chronic morphine makes the mu opioid receptor switch its coupling from Gi/o to Gs proteins, producing excitatory signalling linked to tolerance and dependence. Ultra-low-dose naloxone prevents that switch and softens tolerance, but how was unclear.

The authors traced naloxone's protective effect to a pentapeptide binding site on filamin A, a scaffolding protein. Binding there blocks the receptor's switch and the CREB activation that follows acute morphine. The site offers a precise target for keeping opioids effective.
plos-pone-0004382:
Rhodopsin is the light-sensing protein in the eye's rod cells. It belongs to the large G protein coupled receptor family. Peter Hildebrand, Patrick Scheerer, Jung Hee Park, and co-authors studied its close relative opsin. Their 2009 PLOS ONE paper maps a route through the protein. The route is a channel for the light-sensitive molecule retinal.

Inside rhodopsin, retinal sits in a pocket among seven coiled segments. Light flips retinal from one shape to another, starting vision. The authors describe how a ligand channel could let retinal move through the protein. That path helps explain how the sensor resets after firing. Receptor channels also interest drug designers who target this protein family.
plos-pone-0004482: In 2009, Algar, Muscat, and Dagar found a silenced guardian in a childhood cancer. Imprinted CDKN1C acted as a tumor suppressor in rhabdoid tumors too. Restoring SMARCB1 reactivated the sleeping guardian. The finding opens new therapy avenues. The tumor strikes young kids.
plos-pone-0004582: In 2009, Kumar, Marshall, and Badner hunted autism genes on chromosome 16 anew. Association and mutation analyses of 16p11.2 autism candidate genes were done. The 500–700-kb rearrangement was probed. The study maps autism genetics anew today. The childhood disorder is complex indeed.
plos-pone-0004682: In 2009, Qi, Li, and Rider fingerprinted bird flu in raccoons anew. Highly pathogenic H5N1 avian influenza viruses from raccoons were molecularly characterized. The viral genotypes threatened mammals broadly. The study informs surveillance efforts. The nasty virus infects many animals.
plos-pone-0004782: In 2009, a team tested folate vitamins on CF cell walls anew here. Early signs showed 5-MTHF and B12 helping cell walls in CF. The walls got better fast. The study maps CF care options well. The disease runs in families still.
cowper-john-gilpin-1782:
William Cowper first shared his comic ballad John Gilpin among friends, and it was printed in 1782. Gilpin, a London draper and train-band captain of good standing, plans a wedding anniversary trip to Ware with his wife. He borrows a horse for the ride, and the plan falls apart at once.

The horse bolts, and Gilpin clings on through town and country while crowds laugh and stare. Cowper tells the chase in brisk, rhyming stanzas that beg to be read aloud. Light and endlessly quoted, the poem became one of the most loved funny verses of the 1700s and stayed in print in illustrated editions.
rowlandson-captivity-1682:
Mary Rowlandson wrote her captivity account after Native warriors seized her in a raid on Lancaster in colonial New England. The title page calls the work a display of God's rule and care, written by her own hand. It opens on February 10, 1675, with houses burning at sunrise and neighbors killed or carried away.

Rowlandson spent about eleven weeks as a prisoner before ransom freed her. Grief for her dead child runs through pages shaped by deep Puritan faith. Printed in 1682, her book was the first by an Englishwoman in America. It sold widely and set the pattern for the captivity narrative.
crevecoeur-letters-1782:
Hector St. John de Crevecoeur, a French settler turned farmer, issued his Letters in London in 1782. Warren Blake's introduction recalls Hazlitt ranking the unknown author high among colonial writers. Hazlitt praised his feel for a new country, from a battle of snakes to the flutter of a hummingbird.

Twelve letters describe frontier farms and the whalers of Nantucket at close range. One letter asks what the American is, this new man, in words still quoted today. As the Revolution ended, the book gave Europe its most vivid picture of the new republic and the people forming it.
zola-piping-hot-1882:

Behind the grand front of a Paris apartment house, Zola finds a stew of vice. Adultery, false piety, and social climbing simmer on every floor. machiavelli-discourses-thomson-1882:
Ninian Hill Thomson translated Machiavelli's Discourses on Livy in 1882. The full title names the first decade, or ten books, of Titus Livius. Machiavelli builds his lessons on the early history of ancient Rome.

Longer and deeper than The Prince, the Discourses favor republics over princes. Free states stay free, he argues, through citizen armies and open debate. Even public conflict can keep a republic healthy if laws channel it well. Religion, too, must serve the public good rather than private power. chinese-exclusion-act-1882:
Congress passed the Chinese Exclusion Act in 1882, a first in American law. Chinese laborers are barred from the country for ten years. No prior federal law had banned a whole race by name.

The men who built the western railroads are repaid with exclusion. Labor fears and raw prejudice drive the act through both houses. Renewals tighten the ban, and courts let it stand for decades. jevons-state-relation-labour-1882:

skeat-etymological-1882:
Walter Skeat published his Etymological Dictionary of the English Language in 1882, the fruit of a life's work on word origins. Skeat, a Cambridge philologist, had edited Chaucer and founded the English Dialect Society. plos-pone-0011082: Protein sequence alignments can silently go wrong. This study uses intra-molecular covariation — correlated mutations within a protein — to spot and see beyond alignment errors. The paper offers an independent quality check. The method strengthens bioinformatics. The check catches errors other methods miss.
plos-pone-0011182: Antibody-making cells deliberately mutate their own DNA. This study shows the MSH2/MSH6 repair complex both fixes AID-induced mispairs error-free and drives error-prone hypermutation. The paper reveals a dual role. The finding informs immunology. The dual role builds better antibodies.
plos-pone-0011282: Ovarian cysts in young girls can trigger early puberty. This study analyzes isolated prepubertal ovarian cysts in 11 girls in detail. The paper reveals a pediatric mystery. The finding informs children's hormone care. The care guides worried families. The guided families get clear answers.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1282:
President Truman wrote to Generalissimo Stalin on 31 July 1945, two days before the conference closed. It was the pair's second exchange in the volume. By then the final terms were nearly fixed, and the leaders' own channel carried the last weight.

A late note between the two men could confirm a bargain, smooth a last dispute, or set the tone for parting. Truman and Stalin would not meet again. This message belongs to their final dealings. It closes the leader thread of the volume, as each man turned toward the new world the summit had made.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1382:
The proclamation printed as document 1382 is the Potsdam Declaration, issued on 26 July 1945 by the United States, Britain, and China. It called on Japan to surrender at once or face utter destruction. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

The declaration listed the terms Japan could expect: loss of its conquests, occupation of its islands, and a new order built on freedom and peace. It warned that the alternative was prompt and total ruin, words written weeks before the atomic bombs fell. Few papers in the volume match its fame. Readers meet here the last public offer made to Japan before the war's end took its final, terrible turn.
frus-1945-50-intel-d82:
Russell wrote to Byrnes again on 29 December 1945, near the end of the intelligence office's first season. Eight weeks had passed since his November paper to the secretary. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

A year-end paper from the administration chief often carries the hard arithmetic: what an office costs, what it returns, and what must give. Russell's December memorandum belongs to the season when the State Department began to reckon with keeping a large analysis service it had not sought. Readers approaching the volume's account of the office's transfer and shrinking in 1946 will find the turn prepared in papers like this one.
frus-1945-50-intel-d182:
A memorandum dated 13 January 1947 links two senior offices. The sender was the Chief of the Interdepartmental Coordinating and Planning Staff, Central Intelligence Group (Edgar). The reader was the Assistant Director for Reports and Estimates (Huddle). It stands as document 182 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. The National Intelligence Authority, set up in January 1946, oversaw the Director of Central Intelligence and his Central Intelligence Group.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1945-50-intel-d282:
A memorandum dated 2 June 1948 links two senior offices. The sender was George H. Butler of the Policy Planning Staff. The reader was the Under Secretary of State (Lovett) and Secretary of State Marshall. It stands as document 282 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. The Cold War was turning harder that year, and the new Council and CIA were being tested by it week by week.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d382:
On 20 April 1949, staff wrote up the discussion at the 38th Meeting of the National Security Council for the President. The State Department prints it as document 382 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Reform talk filled the files that year, as the government weighed the Dulles team's harsh grades for the CIA.

Staff trusted these notes because they were made at once, and files across Washington cite them as the record of a talk. For a reader, the gain is scene and voice, rare goods in a file of stiff forms. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1861-d82:
From his London post on 14 September 1861, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is document 82 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Adams wrote as the leaves turned in London and the war ground on. His reports tracked the slow drift of British thought on the blockade and the South. Each one gave Washington a fresh reading of the power that could still break the Union's hopes. The slow drift he tracked was the real battle for Britain in 1861. The drift he tracked was slow, but its end point was the fate of the Union.
frus-1861-d182:
Carl Schurz wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 17 October 1861. The dispatch is document 182 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Two Schurz reports in eight days close the autumn run from Madrid. His eye for character made his letters lively reading then and now. The second report rounds out a file that mixes court news with a young envoy's growth. Lively letters from Madrid were read in Washington with more pleasure than most. Pleasure in reading a post's letters was a sign the post was doing its work.
frus-1861-d282:
Seward wrote again on 25 July 1861, this time to Mr. Haldeman. It was printed as Document 282 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. It belongs to the first summer of the Civil War, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d82:
In a report dated 20 June 1862, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London wrote home to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It was printed as Document 82 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. The letter comes from the summer of 1862, the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d182:
On 4 November 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent a dispatch to Charles Francis Adams in London, printed as Document 182 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It was one of three Seward letters to Adams under that date.

Election day in the North fell on 4 November that year, and foreign governments watched the results for signs of war weariness. Seward wrote through the political noise, keeping his envoy supplied. The cluster of letters that day shows a department working at full pace while the British cabinet neared its answer on joint action with France. Southern agents worked London's clubs and press hard, and the legation tracked their moves.
frus-1862-d282:
William L. Dayton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 2 June 1862, in a report printed as Document 282 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The report opened the June run of the Paris file.

June began with the armies locked around Richmond and Corinth fallen to the Union in the West. In Paris, Napoleon III was weighing a bigger army for Mexico and keeping his Confederate options open. Dayton's reports in this season are valued for a rare thing. They show the court thinking aloud, as much as a court ever does, through hints his letters preserve.
frus-1862-d382:
From Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Cassius Clay, the American minister in Russia, on 4 February 1862. The dispatch is printed as Document 382 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Seward's letter reached St. Petersburg weeks after it was written, at the end of the longest mail route in this file. Clay was preparing to hand the post to Simon Cameron. A February dispatch to Russia shows the Department tending its friendliest channel with the same care it gave the dangerous ones. A habit that kept Russian goodwill in good repair. Russian goodwill gave Washington one capital where it need not argue its right to exist.
frus-1862-d482:
On 4 October 1862 James E. Harvey sent a further report from Lisbon to Secretary of State William H. Seward, one day after his last. It is Document 482 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Back-to-back reports from a quiet post usually mark a case in motion: a ship in question, a ruling awaited, a complaint to answer. In the autumn of 1862 such cases in Portuguese waters grew out of the cruiser war. In that war, hours in port could decide whether a raider got coal. Harvey's paired October letters belong to that grind. They remind the reader that the Union's diplomacy was mostly this: steady attention, quickly reported, from dozens of small posts.
frus-1862-d582:
Thomas Corwin, the American minister in Mexico City, sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 22 February 1862. It is Document 582 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, opening the Mexican file.

Corwin, a former senator and treasury secretary, served the Union in the most sensitive capital in the hemisphere that year. British, French, and Spanish troops had landed in Mexico to collect debts, and Washington feared a European foothold next door. Corwin backed the Juárez government and reported the allied moves at close range. His February letter begins a file that runs beside the Spanish papers in this same volume, the two halves of one crisis.
frus-1862-d682:
William Sydney Thayer wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 13 November 1861. Thayer was the American consul general in Egypt, based at Alexandria. His letter is document 682 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, opening the Egypt file.

Consuls in the Mediterranean ports watched trade, shipping, and the safety of Americans far from home. From Egypt, Thayer reported on the rule of the viceroy and on the cotton trade that the war had made dear. His letters gave Washington a steady view of a land that sat on the road to India. That land grew more key to the war's trade each month.
frus-1863p1-d82:
William H. Seward wrote this letter to Charles Francis Adams on 14 February 1862, a full year before the letters around it in the volume. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 82 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

An older letter set among newer ones is a quirk of the printed file, where stray sheets were placed as they came to hand. Its date puts it in the war's first winter, when the Trent affair's wounds were still fresh. Seward's early letters to London set the claims the Union would press for years. This one, read on its own date, shows that brief in its young form.
frus-1863p1-d182:
One of the Secretary's regular instructions to London, this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, is dated 4 May 1863. It appears as document 182 of the 1863 papers. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

After emancipation became official policy in January 1863, Seward could argue that aiding the South meant aiding slavery. That argument runs under much of the year's diplomacy. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d282:
On 5 September 1863, orders left Washington for London: Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The paper is document 282 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public. It was one of 4 letters between the same men dated that day.

For readers today, these instructions reveal the thinking inside the State Department as clearly as any memoir. They show choices being made in real time, with poor information and high stakes. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d382:
One entry in the running Washington exchange, this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, is dated 5 February 1863. It stands as document 382 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Washington believed Confederate agents used British ports, ships, and soil too freely. Seward pressed Lyons to have his government tighten its watch. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d482:
On 28 April 1863 a formal note passed from W. Hunter, chief clerk of the State Department to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war?

The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d582:
Under the date 1 July 1863, the record holds a letter from Secretary William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d682:
Written on 5 December 1863, this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward went to Charles Francis Adams in London. It stands as document 682 in Foreign Relations of the United States for 1863. It is the third Seward note to Adams dated that same day in this run of records.

Three letters in a day shows how much business ran through the London desk. Adams spoke for the United States in the capital of the world's top sea power. What Seward sent him shaped talks on the war, on trade, and on ships built in British yards. The dispatch rewards slow reading. Its plain form hides high stakes.
plos-pone-0000082:
B. Nelson Chau, Chris W. Pan, and Jean Y. J. Wang dissected the retinoblastoma protein in PLOS ONE in 2006. This protein, called Rb, is a famous tumor suppressor with two broad jobs: it slows cell division and it can promote cell death. The team made targeted changes that split those jobs apart.

Mutant forms that kept one job but lost the other let the authors test each role alone. That split clarifies how Rb normally guards tissues, and which loss matters most when cancer starts. It also has a therapy angle. A drug that restores only the missing function might do, if researchers know which function a given tumor lost.
plos-pone-0000182:
Min Jiu, Xue-Ping Zhou, Lin Tong, and colleagues published this plant virus study in PLOS ONE in 2007. A whitefly that invades new regions is a major crop pest, partly because it spreads plant viruses. The authors report a mutualism between the insect vector and the virus it carries. That partnership speeds up the growth of the invasive whitefly population.

When a pest and its virus help each other, invasions can snowball. The authors document how the virus benefits its carrier, not just the plants it infects. That twist matters for pest control, because fighting the virus and fighting the insect may turn out to be the same fight.
plos-pone-0000282:
Romulus Breban, Raffaele Vardavas, and Sally Blower published this epidemiology methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Its title is a question: theory versus data, how to calculate R0? R0, the basic reproduction number, counts how many new cases one case causes in a fully susceptible population. It is the central number of outbreak science.

Different formulas for R0 can give different answers from the same data. The authors confront theory-based and data-based ways of calculating it. Getting R0 right decides whether an outbreak is predicted to die out or explode, so the paper speaks to every model used in epidemic planning.
plos-pone-0000382:
Marinos Kallikourdis and Alexander G. Betz asked how a mother's immune system prepares for pregnancy, in PLOS ONE in 2007. A fetus inherits half its genes from the father, making it partly foreign to the mother's body. Regulatory T cells, immune cells that calm other immune responses, may help the body accept that foreign tissue.

The authors describe these cells building up in the uterus in cycles. It is as if the tissue were preparing in advance for a fertilized egg to implant. That advance preparation suggests the immune system treats pregnancy as an expected event, not a surprise. Understanding this truce could inform care for infertility and pregnancy loss.
plos-pone-0000482:
Moisés Selman and colleagues described a fast-moving form of a scarring lung disease, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis gradually scars the lungs for no known cause, and most patients decline over years. The team characterized an accelerated variant, describing its clinical behavior and its gene expression pattern.

An accelerated form breaks the usual slow course, overwhelming patients in months. Comparing its gene activity with the typical disease may reveal what drives the scarring engine at full speed. For a disease with few treatments, understanding its worst variant could expose the processes that any therapy must stop.
plos-pone-0000582:
Shonna M. McBride and colleagues surveyed how much one hospital germ varies, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Enterococcus faecalis lives in the gut without harm for most people. In hospitals, though, it can infect wounds and the blood, and it shrugs off many drugs. The team measured the genetic spread among its strains.

Spread data answer a key question. Do hospital cases come from many sources, or from a few strains that have adapted to wards? A few strains would mean a target that control teams can aim at. Surveys like this also track how drug resistance moves through the germ's ranks, an early warning for drug policy.
plos-pone-0000682:
Orna Man, David C. Willhite, Chiquito J. Crasto and colleagues built a framework for comparing smell receptors, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Olfactory receptors form the largest gene family in mammalian genomes. Nearly all of them are orphan receptors, meaning their matching odor molecules are unknown. Judging whether two receptors work alike usually rests on comparing their sequences.

The team based their framework on alignments of the entire coding regions of these genes. A better yardstick for functional differences helps predict which odors a receptor detects. It also orders a huge, mostly uncharted family. For a sense as chemical as smell, such a map is a starting grid for experiments.
plos-pone-0000782:
Sandra Pankow and Casimir Bamberger found a cancer-guard protein at work in a sea anemone, reported in PLOS ONE in 2007. They identify the p53 tumor suppressor-like protein nvp63 in the starlet sea anemone Nematostella vectensis, and describe its molecular function. Until then, p53-like proteins had been found in bilaterians only, animals with left-right symmetry. The anemone is a non-bilaterian, from an older branch.

Their title states that nvp63 mediates selective germ cell death in the anemone. A p53 relative culling germ cells pushes the family's origin deep into animal history. It also suggests quality control of reproductive cells is an ancient job, older than cancer suppression.
plos-pone-0000882:
Jian Liang, Mingui Fu, Ester Ciociola and colleagues examined what the protein ENPP1 does as fat cells mature, in PLOS ONE in 2007. How well fat tissue can grow to store extra energy shapes a person's risk for blood sugar and fat problems. ENPP1, also called PC-1, was already known to play a part in that wider picture.

The team focused on adipocyte maturation, the process by which young cells become full fat storing cells. They asked where ENPP1 helps or hinders along the way. The work connects a single protein to the way the body handles stored energy. That link is one piece of the larger story behind obesity and diabetes risk.
plos-pone-0000982:
James Knight, Bin Qian, David Baker and colleagues worked on modeling the active forms of protein kinases, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Kinases are enzymes that tag other proteins with phosphate, switching them on or off. The human set is huge, and kinases sit at the heart of cell behavior.

To understand signaling networks, researchers need good models of kinases in their active shape. The team use conservation and variability, what stays fixed across kinases and what changes, to guide that modeling. Better kinase models feed directly into drug design, since many cancer drugs target these enzymes. Accuracy here is worth real effort.
plos-pone-0001082:
Daniel Beniac, Shauna deVarennes, Anton Andonov and colleagues imaged how the SARS virus spike changes after binding, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The SARS coronavirus spike is the largest known viral spike. It works like other class one fusion proteins. It must refold to merge the virus with a cell.

Earlier structural work used static fragments in crystals. This team examine the whole spike's conformational reorganization after receptor binding. Watching the change, not just the start and end shapes, explains how fusion is triggered. That trigger is a drug target: stop the refold and the virus stays outside. The work came from the post SARS push to understand this virus.
plos-pone-0001182:
Chromatin, the packaged form of DNA inside the cell nucleus, is usually described as DNA plus proteins. Antonio Rodríguez-Campos and Fernando Azorín argue that RNA belongs in that picture too, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Chromatin structure responds to many influences, from acidity and temperature to chemical marks on its proteins.

The authors present RNA as an integral component of chromatin that contributes to its structural organization. RNA was already known to regulate chromatin activity; treating it as part of the structure itself is a stronger claim. Their work invites a fresh look at how the genome is physically held together.
plos-pone-0001282:
Under the microscope, diseased human tissues sometimes show striking geometric order. Jairo Díaz, Natalia Jaramillo, and Mauricio Murillo document one such pattern in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They describe self-assembly of geometric triangular chiral hexagon crystal-like complexes in diseased human tissues.

The authors report finding this architecture at both large and small scales, mainly in cancerous tissues. They present it as a form of biological collision order in abnormal tissue. The paper is descriptive, presenting an unusual claimed pattern for other pathologists to confirm or refute. The authors offer the pattern as a finding for others to test in their own samples.
plos-pone-0001382:
David Serre and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a hidden trap in gene studies of disease. Most single gene effects on common ills are small. Studies thus need huge groups to spot real links. But if the group mixes roots in uneven ways, false links can appear. This mix effect is called population stratification.

The authors offer a way to fix this bias in large studies with many ethnic groups. Their method aims to keep true signals while cutting false ones. Clean methods matter, since a false gene link can waste years of follow up work. The paper gives study teams a more sound base for their claims.
plos-pone-0001482:
Reeta Rintamäki and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study linking seasonal mood shifts to metabolic syndrome. That syndrome is a cluster of traits that raise heart disease risk. Faults in the body clock had been tied to the syndrome in past work. The team drew on a national health survey of 8,028 adults.

They compared seasonal swings in mood and acts with the traits of the syndrome. Links there would tie the body clock to both mind and metabolism. Such links urge care that treats sleep, light, and mood as part of heart health. The large survey gives the claim a broad base in the general public.
plos-pone-0001582:
Anne Rowley and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on Kawasaki disease, a childhood ill that harms the heart. Its cause is unknown, but a common germ that most children shake off is the prime suspect. The team searched lung airway cells of past patients for marks of that past infection. They found them months to years later.

The marks are blobs inside the cells that hold RNA. Their long stay hints the agent, or its traces, linger long past the acute ill. Lingering traces could help name the agent at last. They also give a tissue mark to test in future cases.
plos-pone-0001682:
Karen E. James, Harald Schneider, Stephen W. Ansell, and their co-authors applied a DNA array method to species that lack genome resources, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Diversity Arrays Technology, or DArT, reads thousands of DNA markers across a genome at once. High-throughput tools like microarrays had sped up work on model organisms, but most species have no such platform.

DArT works without prior sequence knowledge, which makes it suited to pan-genomic studies of non-model organisms. The full text gives the method, the species tested, and the evolutionary patterns the markers revealed. For field biologists tracking how wild populations split and adapt, the tool opens new studies. Genome-poor organisms had been shut out of such work.
plos-pone-0001782:
Takashi Nakakuki, Noriko Yumoto, Takashi Naka, and their co-authors modeled the wiring of a cancer-linked signaling cascade in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. ErbB receptors sit on cell surfaces. When ligands bind, they pair up in various combinations and trigger different outcomes, even though they recruit similar effector proteins. Earlier work showed cells expressing both EGFR and other ErbB members behave in complex ways.

The team ran a topological analysis of the MAPK cascade for kinetic ErbB signaling: how the network's structure shapes signal flow over time. The full text gives the model and the simulations. Predicting how receptor pairings steer signals could help choose among the many ErbB-targeted cancer drugs.
plos-pone-0001882:
Maria Figueroa and colleagues built a joint method to study how genes get switched on or off in cancer, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Acute blood cancers vary a great deal from case to case, and that spread blocks both insight and new targeted drugs. Faulty gene control is a mark of cancer and helps set how a tumor acts.

The team paired two kinds of data. One was the gene sequence itself, and the other was the chemical marks laid on it, which can mute a gene without changing its code. Used together, the two views sort real control faults from noise. The aim is a clearer map of what drives each tumor, a step toward care matched to the patient.
plos-pone-0001982:
Bobo Mok and co-authors studied how the malaria parasite hides a key surface protein, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The parasite Plasmodium falciparum survives by varying the proteins it shows to the immune system. Its main variable surface protein, PfEMP1, sits on infected red blood cells and helps them stick to vessel walls.

One gene for this protein, var2csa, is special: it is tied to malaria in pregnancy. The team examined the default path by which this gene is switched and how its message is repressed before translation. Knowing the switch rules may reveal a weak point in the parasite's disguise system.
plos-pone-0002082:
Stephanie Stotz and co-authors studied how nerve cells sense citral, the lemon scent compound, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. A family of channels called TRP channels mediates key parts of taste, smell, pain, and temperature sensation. More lab tools that switch these channels are needed to map what each one does.

Citral is a bioactive part of lemongrass oil. The team tested it on dorsal root ganglion neurons, the nerve cells that carry sensation from the body. Finding which TRP channels answer to a plant compound adds a tool for pain and sensation research, and may explain some effects of scent oils.
plos-pone-0002182:
Sandra Meidute Abaraviciene, Ingmar Lundquist, Juris Galvanovskis, and co-authors studied how a fatty acid harms insulin-making cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Type 2 diabetes often comes with high blood fat levels. The team examined palmitate, a common saturated fatty acid, and its effects on the pancreatic islets that release insulin.

They traced the harm through a fat sensor called GPR40 and through nitric oxide made in the islet. A diabetes drug, rosiglitazone, reversed much of the palmitate effect by blocking those steps. The work helps explain how high fat levels wear down insulin release, a core failure in type 2 diabetes.
plos-pone-0002282:
Andrea Camperio Ciani, Paolo Cermelli, and Giovanni Zanzotto modeled a puzzle about the genetics of male homosexuality, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Several lines of evidence point to genetic factors behind male homosexuality and bisexuality. Yet a trait that lowers direct reproduction stays present in all human populations at a stable, low rate, an apparent Darwinian paradox.

The authors explore sexually antagonistic selection as the answer. Genes that reduce fitness in males may raise it in females, for example through higher fertility in mothers and aunts. A trait can then persist because the same genes pay off in the other sex. Their model tests whether the balance can hold the trait steady.
plos-pone-0002382:
In 2008, Liu and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits Wendy W. Liu, Joseph Goodhouse, Noo Li Jeon, and others. Its subject is a Microfluidic Chamber for Analysis of Neuron-to-Cell Spread and Axonal Transport of an Alpha-Herpesvirus. Alpha-herpesviruses, including herpes simplex virus and pseudorabies virus (PRV), infect the peripheral nervous system (PNS) of their hosts.

Here, we describe an in vitro method for studying neuron-to-cell spread of infection as well as viral transport in axons. Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002482:
A research team led by Du reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Likun Du, Deborah K. Dunn-Walters, Krystyna H. Chrzanowska, and others. Its subject is a Regulatory Role for NBS1 in Strand-Specific Mutagenesis during Somatic Hypermutation. Activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID) is believed to initiate somatic hypermutation (SHM) by deamination of deoxycytidines to deoxyuridines within the immunoglobulin variable regions genes.

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002582:
Work from Balraj and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Premanand Balraj, Khalid El Karkouri, Guy Vestris, and others. Its subject is rickA Expression Is Not Sufficient to Promote Actin-Based Motility of Rickettsia raoultii. Rickettsia raoultii is a novel Rickettsia species recently isolated from Dermacentor ticks and classified within the spotted fever group (SFG).

The inability of R. Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002682:
Ranji Singh led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was a novel strategy involved Anti-Oxidative defense: the conversion of NADH into NADPH by a metabolic network. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Ranji Singh, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. The reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) is pivotal to the cellular anti-oxidative defence strategies in most organisms.
